sources.note: Recasts long-document visual question answering as building an explicit evidence graph whose nodes are grounded document blocks and whose edges are reasoning dependencies, and verifies the graph causally — masking the evidence it cites flips 82.8% of correct answers while masking uncited evidence changes 9.6%.
sources.title: DocTrace: Towards Traceable Long Document VQA via Hierarchical Evidence Graph Reasoning

sources.note: An Italian proverb benchmark on which models complete proverbs successfully but fail multiple-choice selection when no correct option is present, with CoT analysis showing they name the right ending while failing to notice its absence.
sources.title: Easy to Complete, Hard to Choose: Investigating LLM Performance on the ProverbIT Benchmark

sources.note: A GRPO variant that teaches multimodal models to refuse when a referred object is absent, without losing localization accuracy on cases where it is present.
sources.title: Teaching MLLMs to Say No: Generalized Referring Expression Comprehension via Refusal Calibrated GRPO

sources.note: Separates hallucination into a reasoning failure and a knowledge failure, treats the first with a structured reflect-before-answering format and the second with a reward for abstaining when no sampled chain succeeds, and shows the two mechanisms are not interchangeable -- reflection alone never abstains, abstention alone never lowers the hallucination proxy.
sources.title: REIN: Bridging the Gap between Reasoning and Reliability via Reflection and Abstention Alignment

sources.note: Tests whether systems that translate natural-language reasoning steps into Lean preserve invalidity as well as validity, by automatically perturbing steps to make them wrong, and finds pervasive silent correction -- with the systems best at preserving valid inputs the most likely to repair invalid ones.
sources.title: FaithformBench: Benchmarking Faithfulness of Mathematical Chain-of-Thought Autoformalisation

result.definition: Declining to answer rather than guessing, and across 5 sources a mechanism the archive can only evaluate as one half of a pair. The measured findings come mainly from one system: abstention quality against a 64-sample oracle reaches 78.4 to 83.2 percent precision and 65.7 to 72.8 percent recall at refusal rates of 6.2 to 17.3 percent, and refusals track difficulty monotonically -- 2.1 percent on two-step problems against 14.8 on problems needing five or more -- which argues against a uniform refusal strategy. Its ablation is the useful part: abstention alone raises selective accuracy to 90.2 while leaving the hallucination proxy essentially unchanged at 20.0, because refusing on unanswerable prompts does nothing about errors on answerable ones, so refusing and reasoning better are not substitutes. Two cautions. The oracle defining what is beyond a model's reach is itself 64 samples from that model, so both the training signal and the evaluation share a budget-dependent definition and an abstention that would have been wrong at 256 samples counts as correct. And in one source two ablations that remove the central mechanisms score better on abstention, so the mechanism trades calibrated refusal for answerable accuracy rather than improving both. Where the archive studies failure modes directly, abstention is the rare outcome: the dominant failure is silent repair rather than refusal or reversal.
